                                                        Abstract
     The seminal work of [LMN’93] established a cornerstone result for classical complexity, with
     profound implications for learning theory. By proving low-degree Fourier concentration of AC0 , the
     work demonstrated that Boolean functions computed by constant-depth circuits can be efficiently
     PAC-learned via low-degree Fourier sampling. This breakthrough provided the first sample- and
     time-efficient (quasi-polynomial) algorithm for learning AC0 .
          Proposed by [Moore’99] as a natural quantum analog of AC0 , QAC0 is the class of constant-
     depth quantum circuits composed of arbitrary single-qubit gates and polynomial CZ gates of un-
     bounded width. In this work, we present the first algorithm for efficient average-case learning of
     QAC0 circuits with logarithmic ancilla. Namely, our algorithm achieves quasi-polynomial sample-
     and time-complexity for learning unknown QAC0 unitaries to inverse-polynomially small error. We
     further show that these learned unitaries can be efficiently synthesized via poly-logarithmic depth
     circuits, making progress towards proper learning of QAC0 . Since in finite-dimensional circuit ge-
     ometries QAC0 circuits require polynomial depth to implement, this result significantly expands the
     family of efficiently learnable quantum circuits.
     Keywords: Quantum Computing, Quantum Learning, Circuit Learning, QAC0


1. Introduction
Motivated by both theory and practice, shallow quantum circuits have become central to quantum
complexity. Theoretically, shallow quantum circuits have proven more powerful than their classical
counterparts (Bravyi et al., 2018; Watts et al., 2019; Bravyi et al., 2020; Watts and Parham, 2023),
with output distributions that are expected to be classically hard to simulate (Terhal and DiVincenzo,
2002; Gao et al., 2017; Bermejo-Vega et al., 2018; Haferkamp et al., 2020; Hangleiter and Eisert,
2023). Experimentally, current quantum hardware is noisy and only capable of simulating short
time-scale quantum processes. In order to characterize and continue improving quantum hardware,
it is crucial that we develop efficient learning procedures for these shallow quantum circuits.
     Classically, efficient learning of shallow circuits was an immediate consequence of a seminal re-
sult in classical circuit complexity. Namely, Linial et al. (1993) established low-degree Fourier con-
centration of Boolean functions implementable in AC0 —the family of constant-depth, polynomial-
sized circuits with unbounded fan-in and fan-out. This result had profound implications for areas
such as learning theory, hardness of approximation, communication complexity, pseudorandom-
ness, and circuit lower-bounds. For learning, specifically, Linial et al. (1993) connected Fourier
concentration to the learnability of circuit classes, resulting in the first quasi-polynomial sample-
and time-complexity algorithm for PAC-learning any Boolean function implementable in AC0 .

     A natural quantum analog of AC0 is the QAC0 circuit class, proposed by Moore (1999). Specifi-
cally, QAC0 is the class of constant-depth (shallow) quantum circuits comprised of arbitrary single-
qubit gates and polynomial CZk gates of unbounded width k 1 (many-qubit gates). It is a long-
standing open question as to whether the quantum fan-out operation can be implemented in QAC0 ,
i.e. whether QAC0 = QAC0f (where the f denotes “with fan-out”)2 . If fan-out is in QAC0 , then pow-
erful subroutines such as sorting, arithmetic operations, phase estimation, and the quantum Fourier
transform could be approximately implemented in QAC0 (Høyer and Špalek, 2005). Furthermore,
QAC0 contains QNC0 (the quantum analog of NC0 ), which is defined similarly to QAC0 , but con-
strained to constant-width CZk gates, i.e. k = O(1). Since constant-width gates are what we can
feasibly implement on real quantum hardware and QNC0 ⊂ QAC0 ⊂ QNC1 , learning QAC0 makes
progress towards learning practical logarithmic-depth circuits.
     Recent work has made exciting progress towards efficient learning of QAC0 . Notably, Huang
et al. (2024) established an efficient worst-case algorithm for learning QNC0 unitaries. However,
this algorithm relies crucially on the fact that QNC0 gates act only on a constant number of qubits,
making it unclear how to generalize the approach to QAC0 (with many-qubit gates). In another
vein, Nadimpalli et al. (2024) proved a quantum analog of Linial et al. (1993)’s celebrated Fourier-
concentration result. In particular, they demonstrated that the Pauli spectrum3 of single-output
QAC0 circuit channels (with limited ancillas) are low-degree concentrated. Interestingly, however,
unlike the classical Fourier-concentration result of Linial et al. (1993), this does not straightfor-
wardly imply an efficient learning algorithm for full characterization of QAC0 circuits.
     To see why, note that in the classical setting of Linial et al. (1993), although learned Fourier
coefficients are not exact, there exists a simple projection from the learned monomial onto the space
of valid Boolean functions. This adds negligible time-complexity to the overall learning algorithm.
However, in learning single-output channels of n-qubit QAC0 circuits (Nadimpalli et al., 2024), the
central object of study is an O(4n )-dimensional matrix (corresponding to the channel’s Choi rep-
resentation). Projecting the algorithm’s learned matrix onto the space of valid Choi representations
requires solving a semi-definite programming problem, which can require exponential time in the
worst-case. Thus, the overall runtime of Nadimpalli et al. (2024)’s learning algorithm is far from
efficient. Furthermore, even if the algorithm were time-efficient, it would only describe one of the
QAC0 circuit’s n outputs and is limited to QAC0 circuits with at most logarithmic ancilla.
     In this paper, we address most limitations of the prior work, by proposing the first sample-
and time-efficient algorithm for learning the full unitary implemented by a QAC0 circuit. In par-
ticular, we show that n-qubit QAC0 unitaries are learnable to an average-case distance, with high
probability, in quasi-polynomial sample- and time-complexity. This matches both the sample- and
time-complexity of Linial et al. (1993). Furthermore, we offer an efficient circuit synthesis pro-
cedure for our learned unitaries, making progress towards proper learning of QAC0 circuits. The
key remaining limitation, as in the prior work of Nadimpalli et al. (2024), is that our learning algo-
rithm’s provable guarantees only extend to QAC0 circuits with up to logarithmic ancilla. However,
we offer a conjecture about the Pauli spectrum of QAC0 circuits, which would extend our guaran-

2. Overview of Results and Contributions
The primary contribution of this work is the first sample- and time-efficient algorithm for learning
shallow quantum circuits with many-qubit gates. Namely, we prove the following main result:

Theorem 1 (Efficient learning of n-output QAC0 unitaries) Consider an unknown n-qubit, depth-
d QAC0 circuit, implementing unitary C, and failure probability δ ∈ (0, 1). With high probability,
1 − δ, we can learn a 2n-qubit unitary U , such that the average gate fidelity4 Davg is bounded as

Moreover, U is learnable with quasi-polynomial, O(nlog n log(1/δ)), sample- and time-complexity.

Note that our procedure makes use of classical shadow tomography (Huang et al., 2020) and, thus,
falls within the standard quantum-PAC learning model. However, we use shadow tomography to
learn the Heisenberg-evolved single-qubit Pauli observables of U , meaning we require query access
to both U and U † , with stabilizer states as input and Pauli-basis output measurements.

polynomial time proper learning algorithm for QAC0 circuits. Namely, we show that the learned
unitary can be synthesized in QAC, or the class of all polylogarithmic-depth quantum circuits con-
sisting of arbitrary single-qubit gates and many-qubit CZ gates.

Proposition 2 (Learning QAC implementations of QAC0 ) Given the learned unitary U which

3. Prior Work
Sample-efficient learning algorithms have been developed for a wide range of quantum processes.
For example, studies of generalization in quantum machine learning models have yielded sample-
efficient algorithms for average-case learning of polynomial-size quantum circuit unitaries (Caro
et al., 2022, 2023; Zhao et al., 2023). Additionally, Huang et al. (2022) established sample-efficient
average-case learning algorithms for polynomial-complexity channels. These results leverage tech-
niques such as shadow tomography (Aaronson, 2018; Bădescu and O’Donnell, 2021; Huang et al.,
2020) to achieve sample efficiency. However, while the algorithms are sample-efficient, they of-
ten require predicting exponentially many observables and, thus, are not computationally efficient
for the full learning task. To understand whether this is a limitation of all algorithms, Zhao et al.
(2023) established quantum computational hardness for average-case learning of polynomial-sized
quantum circuits, assuming quantum hardness of learning with errors (Regev, 2009).
     Computational efficiency necessitates focusing on specific prediction tasks or more structured
families of unitaries and channels. For instance, Huang et al. (2023) and Chen et al. (2024b) pro-
vided a quasi-polynomial time average-case learning algorithm for accurate prediction of arbitrary
n-qubit channels. These algorithms are efficient when predicting a given observable on the output of
the unknown quantum channel, for most input states. Restricting to certain families of unitaries and
channels is another common strategy to attain computational efficiency. Computationally-efficient
learning algorithms have been developed for various families such as unitaries generated by short-
time Hamiltonian dynamics (Yu et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2023; Bakshi et al., 2024; Haah et al.,
2024; Stilck França et al., 2024), Pauli channels under local or sparsity constraints (Flammia and
Wallman, 2020; Flammia and O’Donnell, 2021; Chen et al., 2022, 2023a; Caro, 2024; Chen et al.,
2024a), Clifford circuits with limited non-Clifford gates (Lai and Cheng, 2022; Grewal et al., 2023;
Leone et al., 2024; Grewal et al., 2024; Du et al., 2024), and quantum juntas (Chen et al., 2023b; Bao
and Yao, 2023). Especially relevant to our work are (Nadimpalli et al., 2024)’s algorithm for learn-
ing single-output QAC0 channels and Huang et al. (2024)’s algorithm for learning shallow quantum
circuits comprised of constant-width gates (QNC0 ), which we now describe in more detail.
Learning shallow quantum circuits. Huang et al. (2024) gave the first polynomial sample- and
time-complexity algorithm for learning unitaries of shallow quantum circuits with constant-width
gates (QNC0 ). The key insight was that, although these circuits can generate highly non-local and

5. Discussion and Future Work
There are several interesting directions for future work that would strengthen our understanding of
QAC0 and improve the applicability of this learning procedure.

Ancilla. Although our learning procedure handles logarithmic ancilla, many quantum algorithms
require far more ancilla to, e.g., perform block-encodings and error correction. We proved that
our algorithm works for polynomial ancilla under Theorem 4, but proving this conjecture remains
an important and challenging open problem. Concurrent work by Anshu et al. (2024) proved that
QAC0 projectors are well-approximated by low-degree projectors according to the spectral norm,
with guarantees for slightly superlinear ancilla, but it is not clear if this result extends to our setting.
Furthermore, in this work, we prove algorithmic guarantees for QAC0 circuits that perform clean
computation on their ancillas. However, Nadimpalli et al. (2024) also demonstrated that their low-
degree QAC0 concentration results hold for circuits which do not perform clean computation and
even for circuits with dirty ancilla qubits. Therefore, it could be interesting to explore the feasbility
of our learning algorithm in these different ancilla settings.

Proper Learning. While our unitary synthesis procedure guarantees a poly-logarithmic depth
circuit implementation, we believe that proper learning of the QAC0 circuit should be possible. Our
current circuit synthesis approach is via brute-force search and an ε-net, which we believe leaves
room for improvement:

circuits, but also is contained in QAC0 , since it is comprised solely of single-qubit gates and an
n-qubit CZ gate. Therefore, the argument by and lower-bound of Huang et al. (2024) also applies
to QAC0 , concluding the proof.
